newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: FEATURE - Bangladeshi fishermen weather hard times.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Bangladeshi fishermen weather hard times.

text.p: Talk to any Bangladeshi fishermen and he'll tell a tale or two about a profession that's getting tougher by the year.

Most fishermen complain of perpetual neglect by successive governments, but they also say their way of life is being threatened by storms, rival fishing crews from Thailand, India and Burma, declining catches, and pirates.
Despair is growing among thousands of fishing families in Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh's prime resort town, and an offshore island.

"We earn our living on the sea, supply the impoverished nation with necessary natural diet and provide employment to tens of thousands of people," said Shafiul Huq, secretary of the Cox's Bazar Fishing Boat Owners Association.
"But apart from our plight, even our deaths for (official) neglect and lack of survival gear hardly arouses any sympathy at the top of the government," he told Reuters.
Tall but softly spoken, Huq said 85 percent of the 1.3 million people in Cox's Bazar district, bordering Burma, live on fishing.
"We know no other trade than fishing. We can't go to sleep without smelling fish. Some of us are rich, some are poor. But we are always suffering."
Huq and other leaders of his association, which manages more than 500 small and medium-size vessels, said on average up to 200 fishermen die every year because of storms and accidents.
Fishermen said fish stocks in the Bay of Bengal were dwindling fast because of illegal netting by Thai, Burmese and Indian trawlers.
"Hundreds of foreign trawlers illegally fish in our territorial water. They are big trawlers with all modern facilities," association president Kabir Ahmed said.

"They destroy our boats and nets, often throw our crew into the sea and take hundreds of tonnes of big fish. They dump small fish back into the water causing not only material losses to us but also pollute the environment," he said.
The Bangladesh Navy seized nearly 50 foreign trawlers last year but only a few this year.
The association leaders accused the navy of "doing too little" to protect the coast.
They also say a large number of lives could be saved if the government had properly dredged a two kilometre (mile) channel linking Cox's Bazar to the sea.
Dredging was only done once in early 1970s, they said. Now, part of the channel, known as Bakkhali river, is silted beyond navigation except for in high tide.

"When we have a storm signal the fishing boats would immediately rush for the shore...hundreds of boats clog the narrow and silted channel trying to get through, many of them becoming stuck," said Shafiqur Rahman, treasurer of the association.
Ahmed said there were few signal lights or floating buoys along the coast to direct fishermen in distress to the shore.

"Our repeated pleas to the authorities to make the channel easily navigable have landed only on deaf ears," said Ahmed, one of the country's richest fisherman who owns a residential hotel and other properties at Cox's Bazar.
Most of the fishing ships at the port carry up to 18 crew on their usual one-week voyage up to 160 kilometres (100 miles) into the bay.
Storms are always a constant threat during the monsoon, said Shamsu Miah, a fisherman for 26 years.
"As far as I remember I have encountered 21 storms, lost many of my friends but Allah is kind enough to keep me alive," he told Reuters.
Asked why he did not look for another vocation, Miah said: "I would rather die than giving up my profession."
The association leaders were unwilling to disclose the actual size of their annual catch, part of which is exported as frozen fish to the Middle East and Southeast Asia.
But Miah said he earns about 50,000 taka ($1,200) every year. "It's not bad money compared to earnings of the country's overall working class," he said.
